title: Pune's Swasti Patil Wins India's First Gold at European Girls' Informatics Olympiad
excerpt: Listed as 'Unschooled, Pune' in India's official olympiad records, Swasti Vitthal Patil scored 581 points in Cesenatico, Italy, a year after winning bronze in Germany — leading India's best-ever EGOI team result.
body:
• Swasti Vitthal Patil of Pune won gold at the European Girls' Olympiad in Informatics (EGOI) 2026 in Cesenatico, Italy, from May 12 to 18, 2026 — India's first-ever gold at the competition, according to the Indian Computing Olympiad's official records.
  • Her 581 points on the official EGOI results table came a year after she won bronze at EGOI 2025 in Germany.
  • India's official olympiad records list her as "Unschooled, Pune": she learns outside a formal school, and in 2025 she also won an Indian National Olympiad in Informatics bronze as a Class 8 student.
  • It was India's best EGOI team result: Mansi Sane won silver, Diya Sathishdev bronze, and Lyra Floyd Gonsalves an honourable mention.

India's first gold medal at the European Girls' Olympiad in Informatics belongs to a Pune student who does not attend a school. Swasti Vitthal Patil won gold at EGOI 2026, held in Cesenatico, Italy, from May 12 to 18, 2026 — a year after winning bronze at the same competition in Germany. The Indian Association for Research in Computing Science (IARCS), which runs the Indian Computing Olympiad, records the result plainly in its 2026 archives: "Swasti Vitthal Patil won a gold medal, India's first ever gold medal at EGOI."

From bronze to gold in a year

Patil's international run began in 2025, when she represented India at EGOI in Germany and came home with a bronze medal. The same year, as a Class 8 student, she won bronze at the Indian National Olympiad in Informatics (INOI), and her performance earned her a place at the International Olympiad in Informatics Training Camp, where students train intensively in algorithmic thinking and programming.

In Italy she scored 581 points across the competition's eight problems on the official EGOI results table — enough for gold, and a step up from her bronze the year before. EGOI was created to encourage more girls to take part in informatics: contestants do not memorise code, but break complex problems into smaller parts, find patterns and turn their logic into working programs under time pressure.

A team result, not a solo one

Patil's gold led India's strongest EGOI team performance. Mansi Sane of JBCN International School, Parel, Mumbai, won silver; Diya Sathishdev of Chennai, who is home-schooled, won bronze; and Lyra Floyd Gonsalves of PACE Junior Science College, Dadar, Mumbai, received an honourable mention. The team was led by Sonia Garcha of CSpathshala, and India's participation was supported by Sasken Technologies in association with CodeChef — support Sasken described, in its announcement of the result, as producing India's best-ever performance at the competition.

Learning outside a classroom

The detail that sets Patil's record apart is in the official listing itself: where other students are entered under a school, IARCS lists her as "Unschooled, Pune." Her route into computing ran through mathematics. According to Vichar Vatika, the organisation behind the Ganit Manthan programme, she took part in its mathematics programme for several years and later served as a teaching assistant, helping other students while continuing her own training. The foundation in mathematics — logical reasoning, pattern recognition, approaching a hard problem from several directions — is the same skill set competitive programming rewards.

Why it matters, and what comes next

For families in India and the diaspora weighing non-traditional schooling, Patil's record is a concrete data point: an unschooled student reached the top of an international olympiad through the standard national pathway — zonal olympiads, the INOI, national training camps — which is open on merit rather than school enrolment. Students who want to follow the same route can start with the Indian Computing Olympiad's own pages at IARCS, which publish each season's olympiad calendar, question papers and selection process.
